meta.subtitle: Q3 FY26 10-Q: revenue up 86% as AI accelerators and networking ramp, while concentration and a lease Backstop raise the stakes

analystCommentary:
We rate Broadcom a HOLD. The fiscal third quarter confirmed that custom AI accelerators and AI networking now drive the company, and the 10-Q's numbers for the quarter are strong. The question for the shares is the shape of the risk that came with that growth, which the thesis sets out.

The shares sit well below their 52-week high of $495.00. Expected return on our scenarios is positive, but a stall in the AI ramp would cost more than the upside offers, so the label stops at HOLD. The valuation section makes that case, and the final recommendation states what would change it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Broadcom Inc. designs, develops and supplies semiconductor devices and infrastructure software. The 10-Q reports two segments. Semiconductor solutions covers custom AI accelerators (which the company calls XPUs), Ethernet switching and routing, wireless and broadband devices, storage connectivity and IP licensing. Infrastructure software covers private cloud software including VMware Cloud Foundation, mainframe, cybersecurity and enterprise software, plus the FC SAN business.

The company was founded in 1961 and is headquartered in Palo Alto, California. Its fiscal year ends in early November, and fiscal 2025 revenue was $63.9B. The vendor data shows a single consolidated line for fiscal 2025, so this report takes the segment split from the 10-Q.

thesis.body:
The third quarter of fiscal 2026, ended August 2, 2026, showed the AI ramp arriving in the income statement. Revenue reached $29.6B, up 86% year over year. The CEO put AI semiconductor revenue at $16.7 billion, up 221% year over year and 54% quarter over quarter, and guided the fourth quarter higher again.

The cost of that growth is concentration and a new funding structure. A handful of customers buy most of the AI output, those customers need outside capital to deploy it, and Broadcom has begun to back part of one customer's lease obligations to close that gap. Both are argued under Risks.

At $355.14 the shares price in strong growth but not a stumble. We rate them HOLD with a $380–$470 range; the valuation section explains why.

catalysts: Fiscal fourth-quarter results for the quarter ending November 1, 2026, set against the revenue and AI guidance the company gave on September 2, 2026 (see Growth).
New AI XPV tranches with outside financial partners, especially any that bring in a customer beyond the one served by the initial tranche.
Continued adoption of VMware Cloud Foundation, which the proxy credits for fiscal 2025 software growth and which would steady the less volatile half of the business.
risks: A pause by any of the top five end customers, which the company says could have a material adverse effect (see Risks).
The lease Backstop under the AI XPV platform, a contingent liability that grows as racks are deployed.
Tighter credit, which the 10-Q warns could limit customers' ability to finance their AI capital spending.
A wide gap between GAAP and non-GAAP earnings, which makes the adjusted multiples look cheaper (see Risks).

financials.incomeCommentary:
Annual revenue more than doubled between FY21 and FY25, reaching $63.9B, but the path was uneven. Growth slowed to +7.9% in FY23 and jumped to +44.0% in FY24. Operating margin fell to 26.1% in FY24 and recovered to 39.9% in FY25.

The fiscal third quarter shows real operating leverage. GAAP operating income was $15,955 million against $5,887 million in the prior-year quarter, while total operating expenses fell to $4,501 million from $4,816 million as research and development and SG&A both declined. GAAP operating margin reached 54%, up from 37%.

Gross margin was steadier than operating margin: it rose to 69% of net revenue from 67%. Two lines moved underneath. Cost of products sold grew faster than revenue, rising to 24% of net revenue from 19%. Products revenue also included $3,465 million of upfront license revenue with immaterial related costs, against $1,916 million reclassified into the prior-year quarter, so part of the products growth is licensing rather than hardware, and that amount can vary from quarter to quarter.

GAAP diluted EPS was $2.68 against $0.85 a year earlier. We read gross margin as stable rather than expanding, with license revenue offsetting a rising product cost ratio, and the operating margin step-up as genuine leverage on a flat cost base.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Liquidity looks ample. Cash and cash equivalents were $24.0 billion at the end of the fiscal third quarter, up from $19.6 billion a quarter earlier, and the TTM current ratio is 2.50 against 1.71 at FY25 year-end.

The vendor's debt lines need care. They show FY25 total debt of $3.2B and a net cash position, yet the quarter carried interest expense of $778 million, the 10-Q lists "substantial indebtedness" among its risk factors, and the company repurchased $5,641 million of its senior notes in the quarter. Those disclosures do not fit a nearly debt-free balance sheet, so we do not rely on the vendor's net-debt figure and make no net-cash claim. TTM interest coverage of 13.7x says the debt is comfortably serviced either way.

The larger exposure sits off the balance sheet: the AI XPV Backstop, whose fair value the company says was not material and whose mechanics are argued under Risks. A loss at the full undiscounted maximum would be large against quarter-end cash. But that maximum is before any resale value of the racks, it builds only as racks are deployed, and the quarter's free cash flow alone was $13.7 billion. We think the balance sheet can absorb a Backstop call; it would strain only if a default coincided with a sharp fall in rack values.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation is the strongest part of the record. Operating cash flow rose every year from FY21 to FY25, reaching $27.5B, while capital expenditure stayed small. FY25 free cash flow was $26.9B, a 42.1% margin, below the 49.2% of FY23. In the fiscal third quarter, free cash flow was 46 percent of revenue, per the earnings release.

Shareholder returns lean on the dividend. FY25 dividends paid were $11.1B against share repurchases of $2.5B, down from $7.2B in FY24.

The TTM free cash flow yield of 2.3% is low, a reminder that the price assumes much larger cash flows ahead. The capital-light model means most of the revenue ramp should reach free cash flow, which is the core of the bull argument; the stock-based compensation that free cash flow leaves out is covered under Risks.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
Trailing and forward multiples sit far apart because earnings are ramping. The 45.3x TTM P/E is on GAAP earnings for the twelve months through August 2, 2026, a window that includes quarters before the ramp: GAAP diluted EPS was $1.91 in the fiscal second quarter against $2.68 in the third. EV/EBITDA of 33.1x and P/S of 19.0x are also trailing measures.

The vendor's "NTM" P/E of 30.5x lines up with FY26E consensus EPS of $11.66, so it is in effect a current-year multiple, and fiscal 2026 ends on November 1, 2026. The forward frame that matters is FY27E consensus EPS of $19.39, on which the shares trade at ~18.3x.

The consensus EPS basis is not stated, and GAAP and non-GAAP diverge widely: third-quarter non-GAAP diluted EPS was $3.32. GAAP diluted EPS for the three fiscal quarters was $6.09, and the fourth quarter would have to be far above the third to reach the FY26E figure on that basis. The consensus is therefore probably on an adjusted basis, and the forward multiples would be higher on GAAP earnings.

The Street is close to unanimous: 47 Buy and 3 Hold ratings, a median target of $535.00 and a high of $715.00. No peer multiples are available, so we can judge the forward multiple only against Broadcom's own growth, and against that it is low.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: AI XPV tranches beyond the initial one close and AI semiconductor growth continues past the fourth-quarter guide, so fiscal 2027 EPS arrives at the FY27E consensus. The market does not de-rate as the year rolls forward: it pays a multiple a little below today's current-year (vendor "NTM") multiple on FY27E EPS, which lands near the $531.31 consensus target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The fourth quarter lands near guidance and fiscal 2027 EPS arrives close to consensus. Concentration and the Backstop stay as they are, without incident. As the market's frame rolls toward fiscal 2028, it pays a multiple in the low twenties on FY27E EPS, above today's forward multiple but well below the current-year one.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: AI deployments slow: a top-five customer defers racks, or a later AI XPV tranche fails to find financing, and fiscal 2027 EPS lands about a quarter below consensus. The multiple de-rates to the mid-teens as the growth it paid for fades and the market starts to price the Backstop. That lands near the $215.88 low Street target, well below the $289.96 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
The horizon is twelve months. Weights of 25% Bull, 55% Base and 20% Bear give a weighted fair value of $406.50, expected upside of +14.5%, bear-case downside of 39.5% and reward/risk of 0.37x. The rule derives HOLD, and that is our call.

The three cases share one frame, FY27E consensus EPS and the multiple paid on it, so they can be checked against each other. Bull needs no beat, only for the multiple to roll forward without compressing. Base holds consensus and pays a low-twenties multiple as the market looks toward fiscal 2028. Bear cuts earnings and de-rates them together, because a slowdown that exposes concentration and Backstop risk would also change the growth the multiple pays for.

Base carries the most weight because the near-term evidence is strong: the company guided the fourth quarter higher, and the forward multiple already sits well below the trailing ones. Bear gets a fifth rather than a quarter because it needs both a customer pause and a de-rating. A reader could argue for more Bear weight from the price action: the shares trade at $355.14, far below the 52-week high, after a quarter in which revenue, operating income and free cash flow all rose sharply year over year. The daily closes since late August stay in a narrow band, so the fall from the high predates the release, and no source in hand explains it.

The label does not hinge on that split. Expected upside clears the BUY threshold, but the Bear sits so far below the price that no weighting we find credible lifts reward/risk to the BUY bar. The $380–$470 range brackets Base.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The 10-Q reports two segments, and the fiscal third quarter shows how far the mix has moved. Semiconductor solutions revenue was $20,839 million, up 127% from the prior-year quarter, and made up 70% of net revenue against 57% a year earlier. The 10-Q credits "strong demand for our networking solutions, primarily custom AI accelerators and AI networking products." Infrastructure software revenue was $8,752 million, up 29%, though only 13% for the three fiscal quarters, and the 10-Q says the timing and extent of renewals cause variations from period to period. Broadcom is now primarily an AI semiconductor supplier with a large software business alongside it, and the software side is the steadier of the two.

moatFactors.name: Custom accelerator design relationships
moatFactors.body: AI semiconductor revenue was $20.2 billion in fiscal 2025, up 65% from $12.2 billion, per the proxy, and the AI XPV platform (see Growth) is built on the company's custom XPUs. A design built for one customer's systems ties both sides to the program, which is the source of the advantage. With no data on switching costs, we credit the advantage with protecting volume more reliably than price.

moatFactors.name: Infrastructure software base
moatFactors.body: Infrastructure software revenue rose 26% to $27.0 billion in fiscal 2025, which the proxy attributes to "strong adoption of VMware Cloud Foundation." The 10-Q refers to customer contracts without the right to terminate, which give part of the revenue contractual weight. The risk factors also say software growth depends on demand for the data center virtualization portfolio and on customer acceptance of the company's strategy, so this advantage rests on adoption continuing.

moatFactors.name: Margin resilience of the business mix
moatFactors.body: Gross margin stayed between 61.4% and 68.9% from FY21 to FY25, and FCF margin did not fall below 37.6%. That resilience comes from a mix of semiconductors, software and licensing, not from proof of semiconductor pricing power, which the blended figures cannot show. It is not immune either: FY24 gross margin fell to 63.0%. We treat it as a business-model strength that cushions the customer bargaining power set out below rather than overrides it.

moatFactors.name: Customer bargaining power
moatFactors.body: The concentration set out under Risks gives a few buyers the weight to press on price and terms. The Backstop shows the company now supports a customer's financing to secure deployments, which is a cost of winning the business rather than a sign of pricing power. This factor, more than margins, decides who keeps the value from the AI ramp.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. The returns look like those of a WIDE-moat business: stable margins, capital-light cash conversion and a growing share of revenue from custom designs. What holds us back is the customer bargaining power in the last factor above. A supplier with a fully durable advantage should not need to share its customers' credit risk. The software base is the more defensible half, but it is now the smaller one. The rating will move with the breadth of the AI customer base rather than with margins.

points: Fourth-quarter guidance, dated September 2, 2026, calls for revenue of approximately $34.8 billion, up 93% from the prior-year period, and the CEO expects AI semiconductor revenue of $21.7 billion, up 236% year over year. The company cautions that actual results will vary and "the variations may be material."

Consensus has FY26E revenue of ~$106B (+66%) and FY27E revenue of $173.9B, so the Street expects the ramp to run through fiscal 2027. The FY27E figure sits well above four quarters at the guided fourth-quarter level, so it needs further sequential growth from deployments that the 10-Q says are lumpy: fluctuations "may be magnified by the timing of customer deployments."

The AI XPV platform is meant to enable more than 20 gigawatts of compute through 2028. Its initial tranche, launched in June 2026, is $35 billion for more than 1 gigawatt for one customer. The platform could turn demand into funded orders, but each tranche needs outside financing, a dependence set out under Risks.

Margin is guided flat. The CFO expects fourth-quarter non-GAAP operating margin of 66%, "flat from a year ago," so earnings growth from here should track revenue rather than margin expansion. The rising product cost ratio (see Financials) is why we assume no margin upside beyond that.

management.leadership: Hock E. Tan is President and CEO and, per the proxy statement filed March 2, 2026, is not deemed an independent director. That proxy named four executive officers for fiscal 2025: Mr. Tan; Kirsten M. Spears, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Accounting Officer; Mark D. Brazeal, Chief Legal and Corporate Affairs Officer; and Charlie B. Kawwas, Ph.D., President, Semiconductor Solutions Group. The September 2, 2026 earnings release quotes Amie Thuener as CFO; neither document says when the change in the role took place. The quarter's execution, with revenue up sharply while operating expenses fell, reflects well on the team.
management.capitalAllocation: The quarter's highlights list $3,103 million of cash dividends and $5,641 million of senior notes repurchased, so cash went to the dividend and to retiring debt. The quarterly dividend of $0.65 per share was raised 10% in fiscal Q1 2026, per the proxy. The quarter's free cash flow covered the dividend several times over. The new use of the balance sheet is the AI XPV Backstop, which commits Broadcom's credit rather than its cash to customers' deployments. Paying down notes while taking on a contingent commitment of that size is, in our view, the right order.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement filed March 2, 2026, seven of eight director nominees are independent under Nasdaq standards. The Chairman, Dr. Samueli, is independent, and the CEO and Chairman roles are held by different people. Eddy W. Hartenstein, the Lead Independent Director, was not standing for re-election; the board's stated structure calls for a Lead Independent Director if the Chairman is not independent. For outside holders, that means independent board leadership continues through the Chairman even if the lead director role is not refilled. The Audit Committee must review and approve related party transactions. More than 90% of executive officers' total compensation is variable, built on multi-year performance-based equity awards; the proxy's claims of outperformance are the company's own. We see a conventional, independent board with pay tied to long-dated equity goals, and no governance concern.
management.insiderOwnership: As of February 24, 2026, per the proxy, all current directors and executive officers as a group beneficially owned 89,467,014 shares, or 1.9% of common stock. Most of that is the 85,559,569 shares (1.8%) attributed to Dr. Samueli; the excerpt cuts off the footnote that explains how they are held. Mr. Tan held 908,474 shares, under 1%. The five-percent holders listed were The Vanguard Group at 9.9% and BlackRock, Inc. at 7.3%, based on Schedule 13G/A filings dated October 4, 2024 and January 26, 2024, so those figures are stale. No holder is near control. Outside shareholders rely on the board's independence rather than on a large anchor owner, and the CEO's alignment runs mainly through performance equity rather than through a large stake.

idiosyncratic: Customer concentration. Direct sales to one semiconductor customer, a distributor, were 50% of net revenue in the fiscal third quarter against 32% a year earlier, and the company believes its top five end customers were approximately 55%, up from approximately 40%. A pause or redesign at one buyer removes a visible share of revenue, and the 10-Q says losing any top-five customer "could have a material adverse effect." The distributor and top-five shares in each filing are the measures to follow.

The AI XPV Backstop. Broadcom backs a customer's lease obligations to a financial partner over the 5-year lease terms. On a default, its liability equals any gap between 85% of the outstanding amounts owed and what the racks fetch on sale, with a maximum potential liability, on an undiscounted basis, of approximately $29 billion once all racks are deployed. The fair value of the Backstop was not material and no amounts have been paid. The risk is correlated: a default would likely come when AI hardware values are also falling. Note 10 of each filing is where any payment or new guarantee would show.

Customer funding. The company says deploying AI infrastructure "requires our customers to access significant capital," and the risk factors warn that tight credit markets could adversely affect the ability of customers and other AI infrastructure participants to obtain financing for their capital spending. Where necessary, the company says it may also provide residual value guarantees, which it believes would have a low probability of occurring. If financing dries up, orders slip even when end demand holds. The pace of new AI XPV tranches after the initial one is the clearest signal.

Earnings quality and timing. GAAP operating income of $16.0 billion compares with non-GAAP operating income of $20.1 billion. The adjusted figures exclude stock-based compensation, which was $2,019 million in the quarter and which free cash flow also leaves out, so both measures omit a real cost to owners paid in shares. The 10-Q also warns that large orders or delays can cause quarterly revenue to "fluctuate significantly." A widening gap between the two operating income measures would be the sign to discount adjusted earnings further.
risks.systemic: Broadcom operates in a cyclical industry that its own 10-Q describes as "undergoing profound change due to AI." The risk factors also cite trade tensions and related tariffs, governmental regulations and trade restrictions, and dependence on a limited number of contract manufacturers and suppliers. A broad pull-back in AI capital spending would hit the semiconductor side directly and the AI XPV financing partners at the same time, which is why the downside cases cluster. Trade restrictions and the broader cycle in AI capital spending are the macro variables that matter most here.

body: HOLD, with a $380–$470 target range over twelve months.

We would move to BUY if fourth-quarter revenue meets or beats the approximately $34.8 billion guidance and a later AI XPV tranche brings in a customer beyond the one served by the initial tranche, which would ease both the concentration and the funding risk that make the Bear case deep. We would move to SELL if any amount is paid under the Backstop, or if a filing shows the top-five end-customer share above the approximately 55% of the fiscal third quarter while fiscal 2027 consensus EPS is cut.
